title: Chrismation and confirmation
hook: the Orthodox anoint babies right after baptism; many Western churches confirm in youth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the baptism rite: water, a name, a white garment, a candle. Your line was clothed in light. Did getting dressed remind you of anyone who first called you by name? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-four.

An old prophet walks into Bethlehem carrying a horn full of oil. He's come to the house of a man named Jesse to find a king. One son after another is brought in front of him, tall, strong, impressive, and each time the answer is no. Is there anyone else? Well, the youngest. He's out with the sheep. They send for him, and the boy comes in from the field. "Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brethren: and the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward." Oil on the head, and the Spirit comes. Today's word is the oil some churches still anoint with: chrism.
screen: `A PROPHET WITH A HORN OF OIL.`

segments.voice: Chrism is oil set apart for anointing. In Orthodox and Catholic practice it's olive oil with fragrance mixed in, blessed by a bishop, and it smells like nothing in your kitchen. It's the oil of the step that follows baptism. And here the churches split on timing. Orthodox Christians anoint right away. A baby comes up out of the water and, in the same service, the priest touches the oil to forehead, eyes, nostrils, lips, ears, chest, hands and feet, saying the words of the rite: the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. They call it chrismation. The baby is then a full member, and can come to the table. In the West, Catholics, and some Anglicans and Lutherans among others, usually separate the two. A child is baptized as a baby, and confirmed years later, often by a bishop, who lays on hands and anoints with chrism. They call it confirmation. Some other Protestant churches keep a confirmation without oil, as a time to learn the faith and say yes to it. And some have no such rite at all. Both ways point back to the same pages. In Acts, Peter and John come to new believers who had been baptized, and "laid they their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost." And Paul packs it into two verses: God "hath anointed us," and "hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts." Anointed and sealed. A seal was pressed into wax to say: this belongs to someone, and it's been closed with care. Same oil. Different clocks.

Here's the practice: touch oil to your wrist. Olive oil from the kitchen, a little lotion, or nothing at all, just two fingers pressed to the inside of your wrist where you can feel your pulse. Settle, and breathe. Notice the smell, if there is one. Notice the beat under your fingers. A seal says: this belongs to someone, and it's been kept with care. Let yourself sit with that for a minute. If you pray, you can say Paul's words slowly: anointed, sealed. If you don't, just keep your fingers on your pulse and count a few beats. The bell holds the time.
Chrism. Blessed, fragrant oil, used to anoint and seal: right after baptism for the Orthodox, at confirmation for some Western churches.
Your line: sealed. Today, when you touch your wrist, or catch a scent you love, let it remind you that a seal means kept, not locked away. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians are anointed with chrism, chrismation, in the same service as baptism, even as infants; Catholics and some other Western churches confirm later, with the laying on of hands and, in Catholic practice, anointing with chrism.

original.note: Greek: an anointing, oil for anointing — the word behind "unction" in 1 John 2:20.

trapdoor: what you thought: confirmation is a graduation from Sunday school.
what it means: an anointing with oil that seals the Spirit, right after baptism for the Orthodox, later in the West.
what a scholar hears: Paul puts three pictures in two verses: anointed, sealed, and the earnest, a deposit that promises the rest to come.

notes: Editor: 'a farmer's house' (not in 1 Samuel 16) changed to Jesse's house in hook and fork; 'churches still use' narrowed to 'some churches'.

Chrism described as olive oil with fragrance, blessed by a bishop (Catholic: consecrated by the bishop at the Chrism Mass; Orthodox: myron, consecrated by a patriarch or synod of bishops). 'Blessed by a bishop' is a simplification for the Orthodox; confirm.
Orthodox anointing points (forehead, eyes, nostrils, lips, ears, chest, hands, feet) and the formula 'the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit' are paraphrased from the rite; confirm.

Western practice: Catholics confirm later (Eastern Catholic churches chrismate infants, not addressed); Anglicans and Lutherans named with 'some'; age not given on purpose. Confirm the description of Protestant confirmation without oil.
The index hook says 'many Western churches'; the script uses 'some' under the claims rule.
'A seal was pressed into wax' is general background for the image of sealing; confirm acceptable.
Original: χρῖσμα in 1 John 2:20 (KJV 'unction'); confirm spelling and note.
